books.section: Topic 5.9 Government Policies During the Civil War
Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Frederick Douglass, “Men of Color, to Arms!” (March 1863)

stimulus.source_note: Frederick Douglass, “Men of Color, to Arms!”, speech delivered March 2, 1863, Rochester, New York, published March 21, 1863. Public domain. Wording verified against the BlackPast and National Park Service texts. “. . .” marks omitted text between passages, quoted in their order in the source.
stimulus.text:
“When first the rebel cannon shattered the walls of Sumter and drove away its starving garrison, I predicted that the war then and there inaugurated would not be fought out entirely by white men. . . . Liberty won by white men would lose half its luster. ‘Who would be free themselves must strike the blow.’ ‘Better even die free, than to live slaves.’”

—Frederick Douglass, “Men of Color, to Arms!”, speech in Rochester, New York, March 2, 1863

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Douglass recruited Black soldiers after the Emancipation Proclamation opened the army to them. About 180,000 Black men served, yet at first they were paid less than white soldiers. Their protest against unequal pay, led by regiments such as the 54th Massachusetts, best shows that Black soldiers

rationales.A: Background: the 54th Massachusetts fought at Fort Wagner in July 1863 while refusing unequal pay; they fought and protested at once.
rationales.B: Background: Black soldiers were paid 10 dollars a month, with 3 dollars deducted for clothing, while white privates received 13 dollars.
rationales.D: Background: about 180,000 Black men served in the Union army, and thousands more in the navy.
rationales.C: The 54th Massachusetts refused unequal pay for more than a year because they saw their service as earning equal citizenship.
rationales.general:
1. The stimulus ties service to freedom: strike the blow, and be free.
2. Background: the army then paid Black soldiers 10 dollars a month against 13 dollars for white privates.
3. The 54th Massachusetts refused the lesser pay, some serving unpaid for over a year.
4. They were not haggling over wages; they were insisting the uniform meant equality.
Remember: a protest over pay can be a claim about citizenship in disguise.
